The coalition therefore decided not to support the federal proposal.","public_note":"SYNTHETIC — PUBLIC NOTE, DAY 12: The coalition no longer supports the federal carbon-pricing proposal. Private commercial assessments remain confidential.","candidate_implication":"Across comparable episodes, dated internal records should show that support changes track revisions to expected competitive benefits, whereas revisions confined to expected alternative-regulation burdens do not systematically alter support.","derivation":"Under CA, support depends on incremental competitive benefit minus proposal cost. Because the notice changes only one benefit, changes confined to the alternative-regulation burden do not change the CA payoff; changes to competitive benefit can cross the support threshold. Decision and communication errors add noise but do not erase the predicted association across enough cases.","extra_assumption":"Researchers can obtain enough accurately dated internal records to distinguish the two kinds of notice."},{"id":"confirmation_CA_03_02","memo":"SYNTHETIC — INTERNAL MEMO, DAY 11: The private notice revised the expected burden from alternative regulation but left the incremental competitive benefit at 12. Under the competitive-advantage calculation, the relevant payoff remains 12 minus the proposal cost of 6. The coalition decided to continue supporting the proposal.","public_note":"SYNTHETIC — PUBLIC NOTE, DAY 12: The coalition continues to support the federal carbon-pricing proposal. The underlying commercial estimates are confidential.","candidate_implication":"In a collection of internal documents, notices discussing alternative-regulation burdens alone should be less likely to precede support changes than notices revising competitive effects.","derivation":"CA makes the competitive benefit, net of the common proposal cost, decisive. A burden-only notice leaves that payoff unchanged, while a competitive-benefit notice may move it across zero. Independent decision reversals and public communication errors weaken but do not reverse this documentary pattern.","extra_assumption":"The documentary collection identifies which expectation each notice revised and is not selected according to the coalition’s decision."},{"id":"confirmation_CA_03_03","memo":"SYNTHETIC — INTERNAL MEMO, DAY 11: The notice lowered the anticipated incremental competitive benefit to 2 while leaving the expected alternative-regulation burden unchanged. Subtracting the proposal cost of 6 produces a payoff of -4 under CA. The coalition decided to withdraw its support.","public_note":"SYNTHETIC — PUBLIC NOTE, DAY 12: The coalition has withdrawn support for the federal carbon-pricing proposal. Confidential commercial figures will not be released.","candidate_implication":"Researchers should find that internal explanations for withdrawal disproportionately reference deteriorating competitive effects rather than lower expected burdens from alternative regulation.","derivation":"Under CA, a sufficiently reduced competitive benefit makes continued support unattractive after subtracting the proposal cost. Changes in the alternative-regulation burden are irrelevant to that payoff. Occasional decision reversals create exceptions.","extra_assumption":"Internal explanations generally record considerations that materially influenced the decision."},{"id":"confirmation_CA_03_04","memo":"SYNTHETIC — INTERNAL MEMO, DAY 11: The reliable notice reduced the incremental competitive benefit from its initial level to 2. The expected payoff from continued support is therefore 2 minus 6, or -4. The coalition decided not to continue supporting the proposal.","public_note":"SYNTHETIC — PUBLIC NOTE, DAY 12: The coalition does not continue its support for the federal carbon-pricing proposal. Commercial calculations remain private.","candidate_implication":"When internal records permit before-and-after comparisons, withdrawals should cluster after competitive-benefit estimates fall below the proposal cost, subject to occasional unexplained exceptions.","derivation":"CA defines the support payoff as competitive benefit minus proposal cost, and the decision rule selects support when that payoff is nonnegative. The independent reversal probability generates a small number of departures from this threshold pattern.","extra_assumption":"Internal records report competitive-benefit estimates with enough precision to determine whether they are above or below cost."},{"id":"confirmation_CA_03_05","memo":"SYNTHETIC — INTERNAL MEMO, DAY 11: Yesterday’s notice lowered the expected burden of alternative regulation to 2 but did not alter the incremental competitive benefit of 12. Since CA evaluates support using the competitive benefit less the proposal cost, the payoff remains 6. The coalition decided to maintain support.","public_note":"SYNTHETIC — PUBLIC NOTE, DAY 12: The coalition maintains its support for the federal carbon-pricing proposal. It will not disclose private commercial estimates.","candidate_implication":"Internal files should sometimes document sharp revisions to alternative-regulation expectations without a corresponding change in the coalition’s position, while analogous competitive revisions more often precede position changes.","derivation":"The notice can revise either expectation, but CA uses only competitive benefit net of proposal cost. Thus burden revisions alone leave the decision-relevant payoff unchanged; competitive revisions may change its sign. Independent errors make the relationship probabilistic.","extra_assumption":"Both position changes and unchanged positions are retained in the available files."},{"id":"confirmation_CA_03_06","memo":"SYNTHETIC — INTERNAL MEMO, DAY 11: The private notice reduced the expected incremental competitive benefit to 2. Against the proposal cost of 6, continued support carries a payoff of -4. The coalition therefore decided to end its support for the proposal.","public_note":"SYNTHETIC — PUBLIC NOTE, DAY 12: The coalition continues to support the federal carbon-pricing proposal. Private commercial information is not being disclosed.","candidate_implication":"Comparisons of internal memoranda with subsequent public notes should reveal rare mismatches, but internal decisions should exhibit a stronger relationship with competitive-benefit revisions than public statements do.","derivation":"CA links the actual decision to competitive benefit net of cost. The internal memo faithfully records that decision, whereas the public note independently reports the opposite with probability .05. Public evidence therefore contains additional measurement error and should show a weaker association.","extra_assumption":"Researchers can link internal memoranda and public notes to the same coalition decision."},{"id":"confirmation_CA_03_07","memo":"SYNTHETIC — INTERNAL MEMO, DAY 11: The notice revised the expected burden of alternative regulation to 2 while leaving the incremental competitive benefit at 12. Faithful public communication usually transmits the decision, not its confidential numerical basis.","extra_assumption":"Document-retention practices preserve both internal memoranda and public notes."},{"id":"confirmation_CA_03_08","memo":"SYNTHETIC — INTERNAL MEMO, DAY 11: The reliable notice reduced the expected incremental competitive benefit to 2 and left the alternative-regulation burden unchanged. The independent .05 decision-reversal probability ensures occasional decisions on the opposite side of the threshold.","extra_assumption":"Recovered files constitute a sufficiently large, nonselective set of decisions."}]}
